topic: why metallic paint must be mixed fresh (leafing chemistry)
title: Why Metallic Paint Ruins Itself If You Mix It Too Early
description: AI-narrated commentary on the chemistry behind metallic paint's mirror-like shine, and why painters mix it fresh right before every use instead of buying it pre-mixed. #shorts #sciencefacts

hook_candidates.text: Why do painters refuse to mix metallic paint until seconds before they use it?
Metallic paint can ruin itself while it's just sitting in the can, before anyone even opens it.
You'd think paint is paint - mix it whenever, use it whenever. Metallic paint breaks that rule completely.
Picture two identical cans of metallic paint - one gets used in two minutes, one sits open for an hour. Only one comes out shiny.

beats.text: Why do painters refuse to mix metallic paint until seconds before they use it?
beats.broll_query: hand shaking metallic spray paint can close up

beats.text: Aluminum powder and varnish are kept apart on purpose, until the last possible second.
beats.broll_query: aluminum powder and varnish separate paint can

beats.text: Stir them together and microscopic metal flakes rise and align flat against the surface - a reaction called leafing, and it's what makes the paint look like liquid chrome.
beats.broll_query: metallic paint sample shiny chrome finish macro

beats.text: Wait too long and those flakes sink and clump instead, so the finish dries dull and blotchy instead of mirror-bright.
beats.broll_query: dull cracked paint finish close up

beats.text: The shine was never in the ingredients - it was always in the timing.
beats.broll_query: close up paint mixing stir stick swirl
